papers.title: Bio-Templated Zinc Oxide Nanotherapeutics from Flemingia macrophylla kuntze Ex Merr: In Vivo Anti-Diabetic and Anti-Inflammatory Efficacy in Drosophila melanogaster
papers.abstract: Nanotechnology has a major impact on the creation of novel and effective therapies for the treatment of several diseases, including diabetes and cancer. The current work is a report on the use of the aqueous extract from the leaves of the Flemingia macrophylla plant as a capping and reducing agent in the green synthesis of zinc oxide nanoparticles (ZnO-NPs).The synthesized ZnO-NPs were subjected to characterization through X-ray diffraction (XRD), Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR), transmission electron microscopy (TEM) scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and ultraviolet-visible spectroscopy (UV-Vis). Dose-dependent in vivo effects were investigated using Drosophila melanogaster subjected to a high-sugar diet (HSD) to induce a diabetic-like model. In vitro anti-oxidant, anti-diabetic, anti-inflammatory assay, survival, locomotor function, neuroanatomical integrity, ovary and testis morphology, egg-laying capacity, and male fertility were evaluated. The most prominent UV-visible peak was detected at around 370 nm. Structural and morphological analysis via XRD and electron microscopy confirmed the hexagonal phase of the ZnO-NPs, indicating an average calcined particle size of around 47 nm at 500 degree C. The manuscript reports significant anti-diabetic and anti-inflammatory effects in vitro and in the in vivo Drosophila model, together with antioxidant activity. The in vivo results indicate that green-synthesized ZnO-NPs mitigate adverse phenotypes triggered by a high-sugar diet and also potential as an anti-diabetic intervention and warrant further mechanistic and preclinical investigation. Keywords: Flemingia macrophylla; Green ZnO-NPs; Drosophila melanogaster; high-sugar diet; nanobiotechnology

papers.title: Bayesian Stacking of Quantitative Adverse Outcome Pathways Isolates Primary Drivers of Liver Steatosis
papers.abstract: The quantification of adverse outcome pathways (qAOPs) involving multiple converging pathways remains a fundamental challenge in toxicology. This difficulty is worsened by small in vitro datasets with missing values and heteroscedasticity, which limit the estimation of non-linear response functions and the robust estimation of uncertainty. To overcome these limitations, we developed a framework for estimating a Bayesian qAOP Ensemble (Bayesian qAOPE) that combines heteroscedastic dose-response functions with continuous splines and linear models. By combining multiple converging non-linear pathways through Bayesian stacking, the most meaningful pathways are identified, and strongly correlated responses are naturally accounted for. Applying our approach to a hepatic steatosis dataset, we demonstrate by exact Bayesian leave-one-out cross-validation that our framework yields an exceptional predictive performance suitable for the derivation of a probabilistically weighted Benchmark Dose (BMD). Our framework is highly adaptable and provides a chemical-agnostic, mathematically founded blueprint for integrating multiple converging pathways in a Bayesian network.

papers.title: Primary Human Macrophages Exhibit Functional CYP3A4 Activity with Marked Expression-Function Discordance and Cocaine-Induced Catalytic Activation
papers.abstract: CYP3A4 is a phase I drug-metabolizing enzyme responsible for transformation of ~50% of clinically relevant drugs. While extensively characterized in hepatocytes, its role in immune cells remains poorly understood. Here, using primary human monocyte-derived macrophages, we identify an understudied extrahepatic site of CYP3A4-mediated drug metabolism. Macrophages from 100 independent donors expressed CYP3A4 and its transcriptional regulators, Pregnane X Receptor (PXR) and Constitutive Androstane Receptor (CAR), with substantial interindividual variability. Importantly, CYP3A4 protein expression was accompanied by measurable catalytic activity in intact macrophages, yet CYP3A4 mRNA, protein abundance, and activity lacked concordance, demonstrating that expression alone may not predict function. In vivo, CYP3A4 was expressed in rhesus macaque Kupffer cells, further supporting macrophages as a potential pharmacologic entity. We next evaluated cocaine as a potential modulator of CYP3A4, due to its role in xenobiotic clearance. Cocaine had a dichotomous effect on expression, increasing CYP3A4 in some donors while producing no change or decreases in others, a phenotype associated with PXR, CAR, and the sigma-1 cocaine receptor. Strikingly, despite these divergent expression responses, cocaine increased CYP3A4 catalytic activity in all donors, reaching or exceeding levels induced by rifampicin, a clinically relevant CYP3A4 inducer. In rhesus macaques, cocaine also decreased antiretroviral therapy tissue concentrations, coincident with increased CYP3A4 and PXR. Together, these findings establish macrophages as a functionally active extrahepatic site of CYP3A4 metabolism and reveal a critical disconnect between CYP3A4 expression and catalytic function. Moreover, our findings identify interindividual variability and expression-activity discordance as important considerations for personalized medicine and understanding clinically relevant drug-drug interactions in the context of substance use.

papers.title: Human CYP1A2 metabolism of organophosphorus pesticides and nerve agent surrogates
papers.abstract: CYP1A2 contributes 13-15% of hepatic CYP450 content and plays a critical role in the metabolism of approximately 10% of pharmaceutical drugs in the human body. CYP1A2 has been previously reported to bioactivate and detoxify both the thion (P=S) and oxon (P=O) forms of organophosphorus (OP) compounds. In this study, we determined the capacity of CYP1A2 to degrade OP compounds using LC-MS/MS, as well as the inhibition of its activity by OP compounds using the previously developed pFluor50 assay. CYP1A2 was selective in metabolizing thions over oxons, and several OP compounds inhibited its activity in a time- and dose-dependent manner. To further investigate the mechanism of CYP1A2-OP interactions, molecular docking studies were performed using a crystal structure of CYP1A2 (PDB ID: 2HI4). Linear correlation analysis between CYP1A2 inhibition at 10 M with 30 minute preincubation and the % OP compound remaining at 2 hours (R = -0.71, P<0.001) showed a moderate but significant correlation. Based on these findings, CYP1A2 was identified as a potential bioscavenger for OP compound metabolism, supporting the future integration of experimental and in silico data for developing artificial intelligence (AI) / machine learning (ML) models for prediction of CYP1A2-mediated metabolism of existing and emerging OP compounds, including those of toxicological and chemical warfare relevance.

papers.title: Camus: a video-based framework for continuous behavioral monitoring in the mouse home-cage
papers.abstract: Home-cage activity is a window into the spontaneous behavioral repertoire of mice. These behaviors are organized across the circadian cycle, and disruptions in their duration, frequency, or organization may provide sensitive measures of neurological or psychiatric dysfunction. While continuous monitoring can help track the dynamics of spontaneous behavior, video recording in conventional laboratory cages is limited by compact cage geometry, opaque cage tops, and obstructed views of animals, food, and water. We therefore developed Camus, a Camera for home-cage recordings of Mus musculus mice. Camus integrates off-the-shelf USB cameras with infrared illumination and custom 3D-printed components for access to food and water without obstructed views. The modular design pairs continuous video acquisition with a manually validated computer-vision model to quantify locomotion, feeding, drinking, and nesting-related behavior across multiday recordings. A single desktop computer can record as many as 20 cages in parallel at an incremental cost of approximately $250 per cage, recording more than 99% of expected frames at 640x360-pixel resolution and 30 frames per second. Camus captured circadian structure in locomotion, feeding, and drinking. Camus also captured nest-building and sex-specific differences in nest dynamics. Using Camus with transgenic 5xFAD mice overexpressing amyloid revealed selective, age-progressive deficits in nesting behavior. Camus provides a scalable, open-source platform that combines accessible hardware, automated video monitoring, and machine-learning based analysis for continuous and potentially longitudinal behavioral phenotyping.

papers.title: Assessing larger-than rule learning in African grey parrots (Psittacus erithacus).
papers.abstract: Many animals discriminate between magnitudes (e.g., in size, quantity, volume, length) that have fitness implications. Accumulated experience may facilitate the formation of relational rules that can be applied in novel contexts. However, the extent to which animals can form a relational rule, and are able to apply it to novel contexts remains a core focus when understanding the evolution of cognition. Here, we assessed the ability of African grey parrots o acquire the relative larger-than rule in size or quantity discrimination, and if so, how this was learned. Eight captive parrots initially participated in a natural preference test (NPT) to assess their prior preference for a larger amount of seeds. Each parrot was then randomly selected to either acquire the larger-than rule in size or quantity in a basic training (BT). They then participated in transfer training (TT) to evaluate their ability to apply the learned rule to novel stimulus pairs, and a final transfer test (FTT) to assess whether the parrots could generalise the learned rule to unseen stimulus pairs beyond the training range. Six parrots successfully completed both training and the test, with only one parrot, Sensei, passing the quantity discrimination FTT. More detailed analyses showed that the parrots showed varied performance in the TT, but as a group, showed limited transfer in the TT, suggesting the use of associative learning through increased experience in BT. They also showed better performance if a stimulus pair had a larger difference (Webers law). The success of Sensei was attributed to extensive TT alongside his quick natural preference toward larger amounts. These results suggest that repeated exposure to TT stimulus pairs increases familiarity with the stimulus pairs, which can facilitate task success, but individuals vary in their ability to acquire relational rules.

papers.title: Same-sex sexual behaviour reduces reproductive success but mitigates aggression in a subsocial insect
papers.abstract: Same-sex sexual behaviour (SSB) is widely observed across taxa, yet its evolutionary maintenance remains debated and its fitness consequences remain surprisingly understudied. Here, we quantified the fitness consequences of male SSB in the burying beetle Nicrophorus vespilloides and tested three prominent hypotheses about its function: (i) that it provides practice for future mating, (ii) that it reduces tension through dominance assertion, and (iii) that it arises indirectly from indiscriminate mating. Males were observed in same-sex pairings to quantify SSB and then paired with females to measure their subsequent mating behaviour and reproductive success. Same-sex sexual behaviour was common, occurring in 55% of same-sex pairs, and was associated with reduced reproductive success driven by higher brood failure rates. Both males that initiated, and those that received, mounting attempts from other males suffered reduced fitness. Contrary to the practice hypothesis, SSB did not increase mating speed with females and was associated with reduced mating frequency. However, SSB was associated with reduced aggression, supporting the hypothesis that SSB reduces tension through dominance establishment. Our findings show that SSB can reduce reproductive success but may be maintained due to a beneficial reduction in aggression.

papers.title: COGNITIVE HETEROGENEITY AND AGING: AN AGE-INDEPENDENT CILIARY GENE PROGRAM TRACKS COGNITIVE RESILIENCE IN MICE
papers.abstract: Cognitive decline with age is often viewed as inevitable, yet older animals show striking heterogeneity in functional trajectories, with many preserving cognitive integrity despite physiological decline. The biological basis of this resilience remains poorly understood, partly due to insensitive behavioral testing paradigms. Using an automated home-cage platform and hippocampal RNA sequencing, we integrated behavioral phenotyping with transcriptomic profiling to disentangle molecular programs linked to cognitive performance from chronological age. Behavioral data from 906 C57BL/6 mice across 129 standardized studies, trajectory-based modeling, variance-partitioned correlation, and stability-driven gene prioritization identified a transcriptional signature (271 genes) linked to cognitive state independent of age. Preserved cognition was associated with higher expression of genes governing ciliary structure and motility, neurite organization, and synaptic architecture, while impairment was associated with neuroimmune and metabolic-stress programs. A 38-gene cilia structural module score remained associated with resilience after controlling for age (partial rho = -0.81), with consistent effects across leave-one-out resampling. Because the constituent genes were selected on this same outcome, the module-level magnitude is not an unbiased effect-size estimate; recalibration against a null that reapplies the full selection procedure gave an empirical p of 0.026. This divergence emerged among genetically identical mice, indicating non-genetic, discrete hippocampal molecular signatures underlying individual differences. Cell-type attribution against the Allen Brain Cell Atlas localized the module predominantly to ependymal cells, with 27 of 38 genes ependymal-restricted (median detection 90.2% in ependymal cells versus 1.1% in CA1 glutamatergic neurons) and three genes (Dnah9, Dnai4, Kif9) also detected in CA1. The association was not attributable to ependymal tissue content: the module score was unrelated to Foxj1 expression (rho = -0.016) and the partial correlation was unchanged after adjustment for ependymal and choroid plexus marker panels, indicating that the module reflects how strongly the ciliary program is expressed rather than how many ependymal cells each sample contained. These findings support a conceptual shift: cognitive trajectories appear shaped by intrinsic molecular set points rather than by chronological age, with expression of a motile ciliary program at the cerebrospinal fluid interface, rather than the abundance of the cells carrying it, emerging as a candidate correlate of resilience. This approach offers a generalizable strategy for dissecting functional heterogeneity from aging and identifying pathways for hypothesis-driven tests of resilience across the lifespan.

papers.title: Bats Could Learn Three-Dimensional Echolocation Using Echoacoustic Flow
papers.abstract: Echolocating bats can find prey and avoid obstacles in three dimensions using sound alone. They infer the direction of an echo from the way the emitter, the head and the outer ears filter sound, together described by the echolocation-related transfer functon(ERTF). This filter differs between species and is likely to change as the ears grow, so it has to be calibrated by experience. Barn owls and humans recalibrate auditory space after their ears are altered, instructed by vision in the owl and by a so far unidentified teacher in humans. How a bat flying in the dark could calibrate its ERTF is unknown. Here we show that a simulated bat-like agent can learn its ERTF in azimuth and elevation from its echoes and movements alone, using echoacoustic flow, without labeled echo directions or an external teacher such as vision. The agent encodes each call into a structured latent scene, moves it with a physics-based geometric warp and predicts the next echoes through a differentiable renderer. It learns its ERTF efficiently and relearns it quickly after its outer ears change. The results form a first functional model of how bats could learn spatial hearing and yield testable hypotheses for behavioral experiments.

papers.title: Biology Undergraduates Use of AI-Enabled Feedback to Revise Scientific Writing: Recipience and Barriers
papers.abstract: Background: Instructors and education researchers are increasingly developing feedback with the assistance of generative AI, which we refer to as AI-enabled feedback, yet we do not know whether established understandings of feedback uptake and effectiveness apply similarly in AI-mediated contexts. This makes the recipience of AI-enabled feedback a central concern to understanding how to best support students in developing their scientific writing skills. This study examined how two teams of undergraduate biology students used AI-enabled feedback to revise their scientific writing, and the extent to which their revisions addressed that feedback. The teams revised their research proposal drafts after receiving AI-enabled feedback developed by their instructor with the aid of a custom AI tool. Results: Our findings show that AI-enabled feedback prompted actionable revision across both teams. Each team addressed approximately half of the feedback comments, indicating comparable levels of uptake despite their differing approaches to revision. We observed that both teams were inconsistent in providing the additional information and reasoning requested in the feedback, and they struggled to address comments requiring self-evaluation. Taken together, we see that students often addressed the more easily actionable parts of AI-enabled feedback while omitting more demanding revisions. Conclusions: These findings provide behavioral evidence of how students used AI-enabled feedback to revise their scientific writing. The observed patterns suggest that the content of AI-enabled feedback supported meaningful revision, while limitations in students agency, strategies, and volition likely shaped their implementation of comments. Although the degree of uptake observed in this study is encouraging, it is unlikely that a single application of generative AI within the feedback process will resolve all the challenges associated with feedback uptake.

papers.title: Acute and 90-Day Repeated-Dose Oral Toxicity of Urtica dioica L. Leaf Extract Granules in Rodents
papers.abstract: Urtica dioica L. leaves are traditionally used in Indonesia for gout-related complaints, and granules formulated from their ethanolic leaf extract have shown xanthine oxidase inhibitory and uric acid-lowering activity; the safety of the finished formulation, however, remains uncharacterised. This study evaluated acute and repeated-dose oral toxicity under Indonesian National Agency of Drug and Food Control (BPOM) Regulation No. 10 of 2022. Female Swiss Webster mice received a single dose of 5, 50, 500, or 5000 mg/kg granules, and Sprague-Dawley rats of both sexes (five per sex per group) received 77.5, 155, or 310 mg/kg/day for 13 weeks (90 days), with satellite groups observed through a 30-day recovery period. No mortality occurred at 5000 mg/kg, giving an LD50 above that limit; clinical signs, body weight, and rectal temperature showed no dose-related change. After repeated dosing, erythrocyte indices, blood urea nitrogen, and creatinine were unchanged in both sexes. Leukocyte count rose in high-dose females (p < 0.05) but was not observed in the high-dose recovery group, and liver weight differed among female groups without a dose-response pattern. Weight gain at the highest dose differed from control in both sexes but in opposite directions. Control values outside the strain reference range and baseline body-weight imbalance preclude establishing a no-observed-adverse-effect level.

papers.title: Computationally Guided Design of Two Novel Phosphodiesterase-4 Inhibitors for Treatment of Plaque Psoriasis
papers.abstract: Plaque psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory skin disease characterized by itchy, scaly skin. Although there is currently no cure for this disease, it can be managed with medication, such as phosphodiesterase-4 (PDE4) inhibitors. Current PDE4 inhibitors are limited and show adverse effects. With the goal to develop better PDE4 inhibitors for the treatment of plaque psoriasis, two novel drug candidates were designed with computational studies, and observed to have better ADMET properties compared to Roflumilast. A homology analysis was performed to determine the best model organism for preclinical studies of the novel candidates.

papers.title: Breaking Symmetry in Walking: Drosophila Recruits Task- and Leg-Specific Motor Modules for Curve Walking
papers.abstract: Walking animals must continuously reorient to navigate their environment, yet how leg kinematics are reconfigured to produce directional changes of varying magnitude remains poorly understood. Here, we used high-resolution leg tracking to characterize steering behavior in freely walking Drosophila. We focus our analysis on two major strategies, arcs and turns. Although arc and turn trajectories are statistically separable, several parameters suggest an underlying spatial continuum spanning both behavioral categories, involving a change in the steering mechanism rather than a discontinuity in the kinematic space. Arcs, representing shallow curves, and were generated primarily through: (1) graded shifts in the posterior extreme position (PEPs) of the front and inside middle legs, and bilateral asymmetries in stance amplitude, lengthening on the outside (2) and shortening on the inside (3) while step timing and ipsilateral coordination remained at straight-walking baseline. Turns, in contrast, were associated with higher steering demands and relied on: (4) progressive displacement of the anterior extreme positions (AEPs) in front and middle legs, (5) extreme reduction of inside middle and hind leg amplitudes to anchor the turning pivot, (6) skipped steps of inside middle and hind legs, (7) lateral steps of inside middle legs, and (8) spontaneous appearance of synchronized backward-stepping in particular legs beyond a critical turning threshold. Finally, a common kinematic configuration emerges at maximal turning demand. These results suggest a hierarchical, bipartite organization of steering: PEP- and AEP-driven mechanisms operating across moderate and severe trajectory curvatures, and a shared saturated motor state at the behavioral extreme that links descending steering commands to segment-specific leg kinematics in a freely walking insect

papers.title: Reduced food accessibility enhances value-based decision-making in rats
papers.abstract: Finding nutrients regularly is critical for survival; therefore, most animals invest a large portion of their time and energy in securing access to food. Food acquisition activates the brain's reward system, enhancing motivation and thereby increasing chances to succeed again in the future. However, little is known about the effect of food accessibility on cognition. We hypothesize that reducing food accessibility by requiring laboratory animals to get it with effort, will expose them to daily learning challenges, enhance reward system engagement and consequently have a positive impact on cognitive performance. To test whether effortful access to food confers cognitive benefits, one group of rats was housed with a food dispenser specifically designed to reduce food accessibility (Low Accessibility, LA). The comparison group had free access to food at any time (High Accessibility, HA). Both groups were trained in a value-based task in which they were required to choose between two options and, through trial and error, learn which option was more likely to deliver a reward. We found that both groups learned the task structure similarly. However, the LA group showed a higher proportion of optimal choices throughout training, indicating better task performance. We also found that LA rats were more sensitive to the outcomes of previous decisions. Collectively, our findings suggest that reducing food accessibility improves value-based decision-making, potentially by increasing sensitivity to action outcomes, highlighting a previously underappreciated link between food acquisition demands and cognitive performance.

papers.title: Chronic fentanyl induces sex-specific anxiolytic-like effects in opioid-dependent rats
papers.abstract: Fentanyl is used as a treatment for severe pain, and it is a major contributor to opioid misuse and overdose fatalities. While it has been established that opioids are widely misused for their euphoric effects, little is known about the effects of chronic fentanyl exposure on anxiety-like behavior. We determined the effects of chronic fentanyl on anxiety-like behavior, locomotor activity, dependence, and body weight in adult male and female Wistar rats (n = 8 per sex and treatment) that received saline or fentanyl (0.6 mg/kg/day) via minipumps. Locomotor activity was measured in a small open field (SOF) before pump implantation. After implantation, rats were retested in the SOF, evaluated for anxiety-like behavior in the elevated plus-maze (EPM) and large open field (LOF), and it was determined if they were opioid dependent by counting somatic withdrawal signs. Fentanyl increased locomotor activity in the SOF and the LOF. In the EPM, fentanyl increased open-arm time in males but not in females. In the LOF, fentanyl increased entries into, and shortened the latency to enter, the anxiogenic inner zones, most prominently in females. Naloxone precipitated a somatic withdrawal syndrome in fentanyl-treated rats of both sexes, and fentanyl prevented body weight gain in males and attenuated it in females. To provide insight into the behavior across the LOF and EPM, an additional correlational analysis was conducted. In saline-treated males, but not females, anxiety-related measures were correlated between the two tests. Rats that made more open-arm entries in the EPM made more entries into, and spent more time in, the center zone of the LOF (r = 0.78 and 0.75), and the percentage of time on the open arms correlated with time spent in the middle zone of the LOF (r = 0.73). In conclusion, fentanyl decreases anxiety-like behavior in opioid dependent animals. These findings have significant implications as they suggest that dependent individuals might continue to misuse fentanyl for its anxiolytic effects. Furthermore, patients treated with chronic fentanyl for severe pain and comorbid anxiety might continue to benefit from the drug's anxiolytic effects.

papers.title: Lipid nanoparticle shape and morphology determine the magnitude and duration of mRNA transfection
papers.abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNP) are widely used for nucleic acid delivery, with current optimization efforts mainly focusing on refining formulation features, enabling extrahepatic targeting, and improving therapeutic efficacy. Particle shape and internal architecture are variables often overlooked in LNP design, although they critically influence particle stability, biodistribution, cellular uptake, and transfection. Here, we investigate how formulation and process parameters impact LNP shape, morphology, and internal structure, and how these structural features, in turn, influence mRNA loading, cell uptake, and expression. We demonstrate that modulation of lipid composition by increasing DSPC content drives a transition from compact spherical to vesicular non-spherical morphologies, with altered RNA loading at the single-particle level. While non-spherical LNP exhibited higher cellular uptake than spherical LNP, it was identified that this increase was relatively modest compared with the substantially higher and sustained protein expression for non-spherical structures. This suggests that increased uptake alone cannot explain the enhanced transfection performance. The trend was conserved across LNP formulations comprising clinically relevant ionizable lipids SM-102, ALC-0315 and DLin-MC3-DMA. Taken together, these findings establish LNP shape and internal morphology as functionally relevant design variables that should be considered in the design of next-generation LNP with improved mRNA delivery and expression.

papers.title: Small-molecule ACOD1 inhibition attenuates colitis and tumor growth through a shared myeloid mechanism, diverging from genetic deletion
papers.abstract: Aconitate decarboxylase 1 (ACOD1), the enzyme responsible for synthesis of the immunometabolite itaconate, is widely regarded as an anti-inflammatory brake on tissue damage based on Acod1-deficient mice and itaconate supplementation expermiments. ERG344, a small-molecule ACOD1 inhibitor, suppressed itaconate synthesis in endotoxemic mice and in inflamed colonic mucosa and, contrary to genetic-deletion studies, attenuated acute DSS colitis in an ACOD1-dependent manner. ERG344 treatment was associated with reduced influx of immature monocytes early on and accumulation of mature neutrophils. In syngeneic tumor models, ERG344 prolonged survival and increased tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes and antigen-presenting dendritic cells. Across murine and human colitis scRNA-seq datasets and a ten-model syngeneic tumor atlas, ACOD1 marked interferon-stimulated immature monocytes and maturing neutrophils, and tracked with SOD2 and CD274 independently of interferon and NF-{kappa}B signaling. ACOD1 appears to act through a common myeloid recruitment and maturation mechanism, making pharmacological ACOD1 inhibition a viable therapeutic strategy in colitis and cancer.

papers.title: Differential Protection against Acetaminophen-induced Liver and Kidney Injury by N-Acetylcysteine and Fomepizole in Female Mice
papers.abstract: Acetaminophen (APAP) overdose is the leading cause of acute liver failure and is frequently complicated by acute kidney injury (AKI), which worsens clinical outcomes. Although N-acetylcysteine (NAC) effectively attenuates APAP-induced hepatotoxicity by restoring hepatic glutathione (GSH), its efficacy against AKI remains limited, suggesting distinct mechanisms of renal injury. We investigated the role of GSH homeostasis and potential beneficial effects of NAC and Fomepizole (4-methylpyrazole) in APAP-induced liver and kidney injury using female C57BL/6J mice, which naturally lack renal CYP2E1 expression and therefore provide a unique model to examine nephrotoxicity independent of renal CYP2E1-mediated bioactivation. Female mice received APAP (300 or 600 mg/kg) with or without buthionine sulfoximine (BSO, 50 mg/kg) to inhibit GSH synthesis, NAC (500 mg/kg) to promote GSH recovery, or Fomepizole (50 mg/kg) to inhibit CYP2E1-mediated bioactivation. APAP overdose caused severe hepatotoxicity, whereas kidney injury remained minimal during the first 24 h. Although BSO markedly enhanced hepatic GSH depletion and liver injury, it did not significantly worsen renal dysfunction or tubular injury. In contrast, NAC substantially reduced liver injury and improved survival after severe APAP overdose; yet renal dysfunction progressed by 48 h, accompanied by tubular vacuolation, increased KIM-1 and osteopontin expression, and tubular cell death. Fomepizole substantially protected both organs from injury. These findings demonstrate that delayed APAP-induced AKI can develop independent of the severity of liver injury, even with effective NAC-mediated hepatoprotection. On the other hand, Fomepizole protects against AKI in female mice by a CYP2E1-independent mechanism.

papers.title: Macrophage-Derived 25-Hydroxycholesterol Drives Statin-Associated Acute Kidney Injury
papers.abstract: Although acute kidney injury (AKI) has been implicated as a potential adverse effect of statin therapy, experimental evidence supporting this association remains limited. Here, we investigated whether elevated levels of 25-hydroxycholesterol (25-HC), an oxysterol produced by activated macrophages and monocytes, increase susceptibility to statin-induced AKI. We found that atorvastatin and fluvastatin induced cell death in proximal tubular cells when combined with 25-HC. Consistently, administration of low-dose lipopolysaccharide triggered AKI in statin-treated mice. Mechanistically, impaired protein prenylation disrupted the autophagosome-lysosome pathway in proximal tubular cells. AKI was attenuated by mevalonate supplementation, which restored protein prenylation, and by macrophage/monocyte depletion, which reduced the cellular sources of 25-HC. Furthermore, combined exposure to fluvastatin and 25-HC increased kidney injury molecule-1 (KIM-1) expression in human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived kidney organoids. Together, these findings suggest that elevated macrophage-derived 25-HC under conditions of infection, inflammation, or major surgery may increase susceptibility to statin-induced AKI. Our study identifies a previously unrecognized interaction between statins and 25-HC and suggests potential strategies to mitigate kidney injury while preserving the therapeutic benefits of statins.

papers.title: Decomposing alarm-calling behaviour to investigate context-dependent threat discrimination and response escalation in a social mongoose
papers.abstract: Prey can adjust their behaviour to perceived predation risk, which may induce non-consumptive fitness effects. However, quantifying perceived risk in field studies remains challenging as anti-predator behaviours often integrate multiple processes such as encounter probability and detection capacity. Partitioning prey responses into sub-processes may therefore provide novel insights on predation risk perception. To this end, we decomposed meerkat alarm-calling behaviour into threat discrimination, and response escalation. Using 23 years of data from a wild population in the Kalahari, we evaluated the context-dependence of both components in relation to landscape features, and group composition. We defined threat discrimination as the probability to emit an alarm call at predators (eagles) relative to non-predators (vultures) and response escalation as the strength and intensity of the ensuing collective reaction. We found that discrimination varied with habitat and vegetation productivity. Furthermore, larger groups and the presence of pups increased meerkat threat discrimination, but only during the dry season. Response escalation varied with habitat and group size, but pup presence only increased reaction strength. The contrasting context-dependence among the two alarm-calling components support decomposing compound behaviours rather than quantifying perceived risk from a single behaviour. Thus, we recommend future studies to use this approach, when possible, to improve inference on prey perception and responses to risk.

papers.title: Predator sounds disrupt visual attention in jumping spiders
papers.abstract: Perception in one sensory modality can influence not only what animals attend to in another, but also whether animals increase their vigilance or remain engaged with ongoing sensory stimuli at all. Jumping spiders (Salticidae) are highly visual animals, but they are also alert to auditory cues. Previous work has shown that jumping spiders respond to the sound of the wingbeats of wasps, a potential predator, by freezing. Here, we examined whether wasp sounds influence eye movements, an indicator of visual attention. We used a custom-built eye tracker to measure the gaze direction of the movable, high-acuity principal eyes, and tested whether spiders would shift their gaze toward the location of a threat. In Experiment 1, when spiders were played the sound of a buzzing wasp, their retinas, initially at rest, immediately began sweeping rapidly back and forth, but were not directed toward the location of the sound. In Experiment 2, spiders scanning a salient prey stimulus (a cricket silhouette) with their principal eyes were simultaneously presented with a wasp sound and the appearance of a visual distractor. Compared to trials in which the same spiders were shown the distractor without sound, spiders were more likely to shift their gaze away from the cricket but were no more likely to redirect their gaze toward the distractor. Because acoustic cues from aerial predators may indicate immediate danger without providing reliable spatial information, orienting toward the wrong target may be costly under high uncertainty. Our results demonstrate that predator sounds do not spatially guide visual attention in jumping spiders, but instead disrupt attention to salient visual stimuli by increasing non-directed eye movements.

papers.title: De novo macrocyclic peptide discovery produces potent class A GPCR ligands with diverse pharmacology
papers.abstract: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) represent one of the largest protein families of therapeutic importance, as over one third of all currently approved drugs target GPCRs. A growing proportion of GPCR drugs are peptides. However, class A GPCRs (over 80% of clinically studied targets) are underexploited as peptide targets, presumably since their only structured domain is the core, seven-helix, integral membrane fold presenting a limited solvent-exposed surface area. Screening libraries of de novo macrocyclic peptides have allowed for the targeting of otherwise intractable proteins, but their potential to generate selective ligands for class A GPCRs has not been demonstrated. Here, we used random nonstandard peptides integrated discovery (RaPID) to identify de novo macrocyclic peptide ligands targeting the chemokine receptor CXCR4. CXCR4 regulates cell migration, immune surveillance, and inflammation, making it an important therapeutic target for multiple diseases. We discovered novel, potent CXCR4-selective antagonists binding within the orthosteric pocket with nanomolar affinity. The most active peptides effectively inhibited receptor signaling, suppressed chemokine-driven cell migration, and blocked CXCR4-driven HIV entry. Our results show that even the structurally minimal class A GPCRs are viable targets for de novo cyclic peptide discovery, highlighting the potential for uncovering ligands towards other members of the GPCR superfamily.

papers.title: Development of CYP8B1-specific inhibitors for metabolic diseases
papers.abstract: Changes in bile acids (BAs) balance lead to various metabolic diseases, yet current treatment options targeting these changes remain severely limited. CYP8B1 (cytochrome P450, family 8, subfamily B, polypeptide 1) is a liver-exclusive enzyme that controls the synthesis of 12-hydroxylated (12-OH) BAs. Inhibiting CYP8B1 is an attractive therapeutic strategy for attenuating 12-OH BA levels, remodeling the gut microbiota and thereby ameliorating metabolic diseases. CYP8B1-specific inhibitors are currently lacking due to structural similarities between the active site of CYP8B1 and other CYPs, and the lack of suitable high-throughput screening (HTS) assays. Herein, we developed a highly sensitive, and specific enzyme-coupled fluorescence assay to detect CYP8B1 activity, making it ideal for HTS. Employing this assay, structure-based drug design by protein X-ray crystallography, structure-activity relationship (SAR) analyses, and in vitro and in vivo validation, we developed novel CYP8B1-specific small molecule inhibitors. The lead candidate alters BA composition, favorably remodels the gut microbiota, and corrects metabolic disease in a metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) mouse model. These findings reveal that pharmacologically inhibiting CYP8B1 is able to reshape the BA and gut microbiota profiles and effectively ameliorates metabolic diseases. Overall, CYP8B1-specific inhibitors represent a first-in-class promising, safe and effective therapeutic strategy against metabolic disorders.

papers.title: N-Acetylglucosamine ameliorates knee osteoarthritis by enhancing UDP-GlcNAc conversion and chondrocyte DNA repair capacity
papers.abstract: Background: Knee osteoarthritis (KOA) is a degenerative joint disease characterized by progressive cartilage degradation and synovial inflammation, while current therapies offer only symptomatic relief. This study aimed to determine whether N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) is superior to glucosamine hydrochloride (GlcN{middle dot}HCl) in slowing the progression of KOA and to elucidate the underlying mechanisms involved. Methods: Liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) was employed to assess serum concentrations of UDP-GlcNAc to conduct a comprehensive evaluation of the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics associated with both GlcNAc and GlcN{middle dot}HCl. Using a destabilization of the medial meniscus (DMM) rat model, we performed micro-computed tomography and histopathological assessments to evaluate structural changes in the joint tissues. Additionally, we conducted bulk RNA sequencing, flow cytometry and ELISA to validate the efficacy of GlcNAc in anti-inflammatory immunoregulation and DNA repair in knee cartilage. Results: GlcNAc achieved higher peak serum concentrations and more efficient conversion to UDP-GlcNAc than GlcN{middle dot}HCl, with UDP-GlcNAc levels 4.57 times higher at 9 hours after administration. GlcNAc significantly attenuated KOA-like pathological changes, downregulated catabolic markers Mmp3 and Adamts4, decreased pain-related neural markers Pgp9.5 and Ngf, and alleviated pain sensitivity. RNA-seq identified 4,395 downregulated DEGs in DMM rats, of which GlcNAc upregulated 2,808 compared to only 391 by GlcN{middle dot}HCl. GlcNAc promoted DNA repair and adaptive immune cell differentiation pathways, and decreased serum IL-1{beta}, IL-6, and IL-17. Four candidate DNA repair genes, Hist1h2an, Poli, Ube2t, and Hells, were identified as significantly upregulated by GlcNAc, with GSEA confirming homologous recombination repair pathway enrichment. Conclusion: This study shows GlcNAc outperforms GlcN{middle dot}HCl in rat DMM knee osteoarthritis via multiple mechanisms, including 4.57-fold higher UDP-GlcNAc conversion, reduced cartilage degeneration, immune rebalancing, and DNA repair activation, supporting GlcNAc as a promising KOA candidate warranting further clinical study.

papers.title: Pheromones induce visuomotor arousal in jumping spiders
papers.abstract: Perception in one sensory modality can be influenced by stimulation in another modality. Such cross-modal effects may arise from multiple underlying processes. For example, animals may be primed by exposure to a cue in one sensory modality and attend to congruent cues in a separate modality. In contrast, input from one sensory modality may result in a general increase in arousal, which in turn influences behavior. Jumping spiders (Salticidae) are famously visual animals but they also respond to pheromones. Here, we test whether pheromones influence visual attention in Phidippus jumping spiders and, if so, whether we see evidence of priming to relevant stimuli or simply an increase in arousal. In Experiment 1, male spiders exposed to female pheromones increased their movements in an arena, a sign of physiological arousal associated with mate searching, whereas females decreased their movements in response to male pheromones. In Experiment 2, freely moving male spiders exposed to female pheromones were more likely to detect and court an image of a female. In Experiment 3, male spiders were shown a series of images of conspecifics, crickets, and abstract shapes as we visualized the gaze direction of their principal eyes using a specialized eyetracker. When pheromones were present, retinal movement markedly increased, but this effect did not differ by stimulus category. Spiders showed greater retinal movement during presentations of crickets and front-facing female conspecifics than during presentations of side-view male conspecifics, regardless of pheromone exposure. In Experiment 4, spiders were shown an array of stimuli, but spiders did not preferentially look at a conspecific stimulus with pheromone exposure. In a second iteration of Experiment 4 with male spiders tested in both control and pheromone conditions, however, pheromone-exposed males looked longer at a front-facing female than at an abstract shape. In Experiment 5, spiders were presented with a salient image of a conspecific of the opposite sex. With pheromone exposure, males were more likely to divert their gaze away from the initial stimulus to an oval distractor, while females were less likely to divert their gaze than controls, mirroring sex-specific shifts in activity from Experiment 1. Increased male movement may enhance encounters, whereas reduced female movement may facilitate being found and evaluating male displays. While we found only limited evidence that spiders were primed to direct their attention toward congruent stimuli, our results show pheromones influence vision, specifically by affecting the spiders' propensity to move their bodies and eyes.

papers.title: Discovery of a brain-penetrant CHI3L1 inhibitor as an oral modulator of neuroinflammation in Alzheimers disease
papers.abstract: Chitinase-3-like protein 1 (CHI3L1) is elevated in Alzheimers disease (AD), but its role in glial dysfunction and therapeutic tractability remain unclear. Here, screening a 4.2-billion-compound DNA-encoded library identified DELC2, a brain-penetrant CHI3L1 modulator. Biophysical and crystallographic studies showed that DELC2 binds the CHI3L1 glycan-recognition groove within an aromatic-hydrophobic pocket centered on Trp99 and Trp352. DELC2 inhibited CHI3L1-RAGE association, suppressed CHI3L1-induced inflammatory signaling, reduced Gal-3-positive microglia, and restored amyloid-{beta} uptake in glial cultures. In human cerebrospinal fluid, CHI3L1 was elevated in AD and correlated with astrocytic NF-{kappa}B activation. DELC2 phenocopied CHI3L1 immunodepletion, whereas CHI3L1 add-back restored inflammatory and amyloid-{beta}-handling defects. Oral DELC2 achieved sustained unbound brain exposure in 5xFAD mice, improved cognitive performance, reduced multiple amyloid-{beta} species, and attenuated astrocytic and microglial inflammatory programs. These findings establish the CHI3L1 glycan-recognition groove as a druggable regulator of RAGE-associated glial dysfunction and identify DELC2 as a chemical scaffold for CHI3L1-directed therapy in AD.

papers.title: Livestock depredation frequency is negatively associated with wolf body mass
papers.abstract: Foraging theory predicts that behavioral decisions are state-dependent, with individuals expected to alter foraging strategies according to physiological condition. Although livestock depredation by carnivores is often attributed to seasonal changes in prey availability and livestock exposure, less attention has been given to predator state. We evaluated whether seasonal variation in wolf body mass was associated with monthly livestock depredation frequency using 17 years of monitoring data from gray wolves (Canis lupus) in Oregon, USA. Using 329 body-mass measurements from 274 wolves, we modeled age- and season-related variation in body mass and generated standardized monthly population-level predictions. Predicted body mass declined through spring and summer, reached its lowest values in late summer, and increased into winter. Monthly depredation frequency decreased as predicted population-level body mass increased; a one-standard-deviation increase in predicted mass was associated with a 36.7% decrease in expected monthly depredation frequency (95% confidence interval: 22.7-48.1% decrease). The negative association persisted across sensitivity analyses based on predicted population-level body mass. When season was modeled explicitly, the association remained negative, but uncertainty increased substantially because predicted body mass and season contained limited independent temporal information. Livestock depredations were therefore most frequent during the portion of the annual cycle when wolves were predicted to have their lowest body mass. The observed association is consistent with state-dependent foraging theory, but the available data could not determine whether body mass itself contributed to depredation frequency or whether other seasonal ecological processes drove the association. Our results identify predator state as a potentially important but understudied component of carnivore-livestock interactions. Integrating measures of predator state with established drivers of conflict, including livestock exposure, husbandry, native prey, and landscape conditions, may help determine whether predator state provides additional information for understanding and anticipating carnivore-livestock conflict.

papers.title: Males of a suboscine lekking bird exhibit neighbor-stranger discrimination
papers.abstract: The ability to discriminate the vocalizations of neighbors from strangers is one way individuals can reduce conflict and minimize the associated physical and energetic costs. Although individual vocal variation and neighbor-stranger discrimination has been tested across various taxa, within birds, it is more commonly investigated in oscine passerines and territorial species, while suboscine passerines and lekking species are often neglected. Red-capped manakins, Ceratopipra mentalis, are a suboscine lekking bird that is known to exhibit individual variation in their whistle-peep vocalizations. We performed a playback experiment at C. mentalis leks to evaluate whether they exhibit neighbor-stranger discrimination at the lek-scale. We found that C. mentalis males responded more quickly to strangers compared to neighbors, suggesting that strangers are a greater threat to males than neighboring individuals. Neighbor-stranger discrimination was only observed in vocal responses, not movement responses, and differences in total vocal responses were only observed when we evaluated the changes in response to neighbors versus strangers over time. These findings add to a growing body of literature demonstrating that non-territorial and suboscine species are capable of neighbor-stranger discrimination. Further examination of neighbor-stranger discrimination in these understudied species can yield insights into the functions of vocalizations, and in particular male-male interactions and mate choice in highly sexually-selected species.

papers.title: Liposomal DAGLβ Inhibitor Shows Substantial Antinociceptive Potency Mediated by AMPK in a Neuropathic Pain Mouse Models
papers.abstract: Diacylglycerol lipase-beta (DAGL{beta}), a biosynthetic enzyme for the endocannabinoid 2-arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG), is highly expressed in macrophages and serves as a potential contributor to inflammatory and hypernociceptive responses. Moreover, the DAGL{beta} inhibitor KT109 produces antinociceptive effects in various rodent pain models, and its liposome formulation dramatically increases its antinociceptive potency in a lipopolysaccharide mouse model of inflammatory pain compared to free KT109. Here, we further optimized the liposomal KT109 formulation through adjustment of lipid composition and improved processing, achieving 100-fold higher drug encapsulation efficiency than the previous formulation, uniform size distribution, and excellent storage stability. Further, the second generation liposomal KT109 showed remarkable potency (ED50 [95% CL] = 0.226 [0.113-0.454] mg/kg) in a mouse model of paclitaxel-induced neuropathic pain, compared to free KT109 (ED50 [95% CL] = 31 [21-46] mg/kg). Liposomal KT109 (0.4 mg/kg) fully reversed paclitaxel-induced mechanical hypersensitivity for up to 24 hours, and its antinociceptive effects were sustained following a week of daily injections, with no detectable tolerance. In addition, the adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase (AMPK) inhibitor, dorsomorphin, prevented the antinociceptive effects of KT109, which is consistent with previous work demonstrating AMPK activation mediates the antinociceptive phenotype of DAGL{beta} knockout mice.

papers.title: The ontogeny of repeatability: measurement choices shape individuality estimates in a clonal fish
papers.abstract: Consistent among-individual differences in behavior across time and contexts ("individuality", "animal personality") are increasingly recognized as playing an important role in both the ecology and evolution of species. Such individuality is not static: individual differences emerge, shift, and crystallize across ontogeny, shaped by developmental plasticity, stochastic processes, and gene-environment interactions. Despite growing awareness of this developmental dimension, the field has relied predominantly on snapshot designs with few repeated measures, raising the question of how much reported repeatability estimates reflect biology versus methodological choices. Here, we leverage high-resolution tracking data from 45 clonal Amazon mollies (Poecilia formosa) recorded at 5 frames per second across the first 28 days of life to systematically examine how temporal aggregation, sampling rate, frame rate, and the number and placement of measurement days affect repeatability estimates and their underlying variance components. We find that repeatability increases with higher temporal aggregation, decreases with lower sampling rates, and varies substantially depending on the developmental stage sampled. These results demonstrate that commonly used measurement practices can substantially distort repeatability estimates, and that conclusions about behavioral consistency may be as much a product of study design as of biology. We close with practical recommendations for researchers studying individuality across development.
